common_name: Russian Rhapsody Daylily (Violet-Purple Rebloomer with Gold Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Russian Rhapsody's semi-evergreen crown benefits from a protective mulch in colder parts of its range.

directions: Registered in 1973, Russian Rhapsody produces richly saturated violet-purple flowers centered with a bright yellow throat, a strong color contrast that has kept it popular with collectors of purple-toned daylilies. Its semi-evergreen clumps send up well-branched scapes about thirty inches tall carrying a dependable midseason bloom with a reliable rebloom flush later in the season, performance that earned it the Lenington All-American Award in 1989 for garden-worthiness across varied climates. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flower counts high.

common_name: Nosferatu Daylily (Near-Black Purple with Chartreuse Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the darkest flower color; semi-evergreen foliage tolerates moderate winters without excessive dieback.

directions: Hybridized by Curt Hanson and registered in 1990, Nosferatu bears deeply saturated purple flowers so dark they read nearly black in bright sun, brightened only by a crisp green-chartreuse throat. Its fragrant blooms open on well-branched, twenty-six-inch scapes during a midseason display, and the semi-evergreen foliage holds up through moderate winters without excessive dieback. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, since the darkest purple tones develop best with consistent sunlight, and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Chicago Picotee Memories Daylily (Cream and Purple Picotee Bicolor)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; dormant foliage dies back fully for winter.

directions: Registered in 1987 as part of the long-running Chicago series of daylilies, Chicago Picotee Memories opens creamy petals edged in a contrasting purple picotee band with a deeper purple eyezone and a greenish-yellow throat, giving each flower a crisp, hand-painted look. Dormant clumps send up thirty-inch scapes for an early-season bloom display before many other daylilies have started. Grow in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, and divide every three to four years in spring once flowering begins to decline from crowding.

common_name: Mary's Gold Daylily (Brilliant Golden-Orange Award Winner)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps reward feeding with heavier midseason bloom.

directions: Registered in 1984, Mary's Gold carries brilliant golden-orange, self-colored flowers over six inches across with a clean green throat, a bold color that has made it a long-standing favorite among orange daylilies. Its tetraploid clumps produce well-branched, thirty-four-inch scapes for a heavy midseason bloom, performance that was recognized with the President's Cup in 2001 and the Lenington All-American Award in 2005 for garden-worthiness across many regions. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every few years to sustain strong flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; fragrance and extended evening bloom are strongest in warm weather.

directions: Hybridized by Frank W. Childs and registered in 1972, Serene Madonna produces large, softly fragrant, near-white flowers with a cool green throat that stay open later into the evening than typical daytime bloomers. Its clumps bloom in a mid-to-late season flush with a dependable rebloom later in summer, giving a longer season of flowers than many daylilies from its era. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide every three to four years in spring to keep the clump vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; mulch over winter in colder parts of its range since foliage is evergreen.

directions: Registered in 1982, Lunar Sea bears clear lemon-yellow flowers with a soft chartreuse throat and a light fragrance, carried on compact, twenty-two-inch scapes over an early-to-midseason bloom with a reliable later rebloom flush. Its evergreen foliage performs best where winters are mild to moderate, since hard freezes can damage actively growing crowns. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, and mulch over winter in colder parts of its range to protect the crown.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage tolerates moderate winters.

directions: Registered in 1962, this historic diploid daylily bears soft ribbon-pink flowers with a yellow-green throat on twenty-four-inch scapes during a midseason bloom. Its semi-evergreen foliage and vigorous constitution have kept it in collector circulation for decades as an example of mid-twentieth-century pastel-toned daylily breeding. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and divide every three to four years as clumps become congested.

common_name: Siloam Ralph Henry Daylily (Pale Blush Miniature-Scape Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; dormant foliage dies back fully for winter.

directions: Hybridized by Pauline Henry and registered in 1988 as part of her extensive Siloam series, Siloam Ralph Henry bears unusually large, pale blush-pink flowers nearly seven inches across held on compact eighteen-inch scapes, an eye-catching contrast of huge bloom on a low-growing plant. The extended daily bloom lets each flower stay open later than typical daylilies, and the dormant foliage dies back fully for winter. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain strong flowering.

common_name: Tuxedo Moon Daylily (Burgundy-Purple with Violet Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage tolerates moderate winters.

directions: Hybridized by Curt Hanson and registered in 1989, Tuxedo Moon bears rich burgundy-purple flowers accented by a lighter violet eyezone and a green-chartreuse throat, a layered color pattern that made it an influential parent in later dark-flowered daylily breeding. Its semi-evergreen clumps produce twenty-five-inch scapes for a dependable midseason bloom. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide every three to four years in spring to refresh flowering.

common_name: Chicago Regal Daylily (Purple with Deep Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage tolerates moderate winters.

directions: Registered in 1970 as an early entry in the long-running Chicago series of daylilies, Chicago Regal bears large, fragrant purple flowers up to seven inches across, deepened by a darker eyezone and brightened by a green throat. Its semi-evergreen, tetraploid clumps send up thirty-inch scapes for a heavy midseason bloom. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide every three to four years once flowering begins to taper from overcrowding.

common_name: Knave Daylily (Rose-Red Rebloomer with Cream Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; evergreen foliage performs best where winters are mild to moderate.

directions: Registered in 1971, Knave carries rich rose-red flowers with a contrasting cream throat on twenty-six-inch scapes, opening during a fragrant midseason display with a later rebloom flush in favorable climates. Its evergreen foliage performs best where winters stay mild to moderate, and the extended daily bloom keeps flowers open later than many daytime-only cultivars. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, and divide every few years to keep clumps blooming heavily.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage tolerates moderate winters.

directions: Registered in 1971, Embassy bears deep burgundy flowers with a soft yellow-cream throat on compact twenty-inch scapes, making it a good choice for the front of a border where taller daylilies would overwhelm the planting. It blooms in midseason with a later rebloom flush, and the extended daily bloom habit lets flowers stay open longer than typical daytime bloomers. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Hybridized by Howard J. Hite and registered in 1973, Creepy Crawler bears clear golden-yellow, fragrant flowers with a chartreuse throat on thirty-inch scapes during an early-to-midseason bloom. It later proved influential as a parent, appearing in the ancestry of later gold and orange daylily introductions. Plant dormant divisions in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to sustain heavy bloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; evergreen foliage favors mild-to-moderate winter climates.

directions: Registered in 1982, Royal Saracen produces light purple flowers with a cream-to-chartreuse throat on twenty-six-inch scapes during an early-to-midseason display, with a later rebloom flush extending the season. It went on to become a notable parent in dark-eyed purple breeding lines, including Tuxedo Moon. Its evergreen foliage favors mild-to-moderate winter climates; grow in full sun in moist, well-drained soil and divide every few years to keep bloom counts high.

common_name: Grand Masterpiece Daylily (Deep Purple with Lime Throat)

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun.

directions: Hybridized by Bob V. Dove and registered in 1984, Grand Masterpiece bears deep purple flowers nearly six inches across with a bright lime-green throat, held on compact twenty-one-inch scapes during an early-to-midseason bloom. This diploid cultivar's rich, saturated purple went on to influence later breeding lines, including tetraploid conversions used by other hybridizers. Plant dormant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and divide every three to four years as clumps become crowded.
